answers.answer: DNS resolves api.notes.example, not /notes/42. The stub is the client's local lookup helper and asks a recursive resolver to obtain an answer. With empty relevant caches, that resolver asks root, follows its .example referral, then follows .example's notes.example referral to the authority. A referral points toward the responsible servers, not the final host address. Delegation assigns responsibility for a child zone; a zone is a managed portion of DNS names, whose authoritative server supplies its records. The authoritative answer supplies the api.notes.example CNAME alias to edge.notes.example. CNAME contains a DNS name, not an address or URL; the resolver follows the target to obtain its A (IPv4) or AAAA (IPv6) data. These may accompany the alias; otherwise another lookup is required. Without usable target address data the alias provides no connectable address. The recursive resolver returns the result to the stub; later cached answers can avoid authority visits, cached delegations can shorten the route, and alias and target records can be cached separately. The client chooses a reachable address family, connects to a usable address, verifies HTTPS for api.notes.example and sends its HTTP request with /notes/42 as the path. HTTPS encrypts the HTTP exchange. DNS does not carry that exchange; an address does not prove Notes is healthy. No unsupported step is required by this trace.

evidence.quote: DNS resolves the hostname, not the URL path, and does not carry the later HTTP exchange.

The stub resolver is the client's local lookup helper. It asks a recursive resolver to obtain an answer on its behalf. An authoritative server supplies records for a zone, a managed portion of DNS names.
Delegation assigns responsibility for a child zone to its authoritative servers. A referral points the resolver toward them; it is not the final host address.
An A record supplies an IPv4 address; an AAAA record supplies an IPv6 address.
A CNAME record is a name alias. Resolving it follows the target name to obtain A or AAAA data, possibly already cached or returned with the alias. Otherwise another lookup is needed.
HTTPS separately authenticates the endpoint through certificate validation and encrypts the HTTP exchange.

answers.answer: TTL limits ordinary reuse of cached answers in seconds; each cache ages the TTL it received. The 11:59 entry received 3600 seconds, so it can remain ordinarily usable until 12:59. It need not refresh by 12:01: the noon TTL/address edit does not rewrite that entry. For a safer move, lower TTL first and allow the old 3600-second TTL to age out before switching the address. Keep the old destination usable through the transition, monitoring traffic, errors and existing connections at both destinations. The lesson supports no exact universal shutdown time: DNS does not migrate open connections and some resolvers may serve expired data when refresh fails. Short TTLs cause more refresh queries and more frequent dependence on working DNS. Independent caches and connection lifetimes prevent simultaneous cutover, so TTL is no worldwide update timer or hard recovery deadline.

evidence.quote: TTL, or time to live, limits ordinary cache reuse in seconds. Each cache ages the TTL it received; it is not a worldwide update timer.

For a planned move, lower TTL first, allow the previous longer TTL to age out, then switch. Keep the old destination usable through the transition while monitoring traffic, errors and existing connections at both destinations. DNS edits do not migrate open connections.

Shorter TTLs mean more refresh queries and more frequent dependence on working DNS. Independent caches and connection lifetimes prevent a simultaneous cutover. Some resolvers can even serve expired data when refreshing fails, so TTL is not a hard global recovery deadline.

answers.answer: Negative caching reuses an answer reporting absence. The earlier NXDOMAIN has its own cache lifetime; creating the A record does not notify that cache, and its new 30-second positive TTL does not clear the older negative answer. The supplied material does not give that negative lifetime, so the exact time visibility returns is unsupported. NXDOMAIN says the queried name does not exist, though the observed answer here may be cached from before creation. NODATA for AAAA says the name exists but lacks that requested type; it does not imply there is no A record or no name. SERVFAIL means resolution could not be completed, not that the name is absent. Failures may also be cached to avoid repeatedly hammering failing DNS servers. Check the queried name, requested type and returned status to distinguish these investigations.

evidence.quote: Negative caching reuses an answer reporting absence. NXDOMAIN says the queried name does not exist. NODATA means the name exists but has no record of the requested type: no AAAA record does not imply no A record or no name.
The negative answer has its own cache lifetime; the new positive record's TTL does not clear it.

SERVFAIL means resolution could not be completed, for example because the resolver could not obtain usable answers. It is not proof that the name does not exist. Resolution failures may also be cached to avoid repeatedly hammering failing DNS servers.

answers.answer: Steering selects destinations returned in DNS answers; failover changes the selected destination after a failure. A separate health check and policy, or an operator, must detect east's failure and change answers: ordinary DNS records do not detect application health. Equal shares of lookup answers do not guarantee equal shares of HTTP requests, because a shared recursive resolver can reuse an answer for many clients and clients may send many requests through one address or connection. Removing east changes new answers, but cached clients can still try east and existing connections do not migrate to west. DNS does not select again on every HTTP request. West must be reachable, healthy and have enough spare capacity for redirected work; a health signal is only a sample. DNS changes do not create capacity or guarantee immediate recovery. No specific recovery time or automatic detection mechanism is established by the scenario.

evidence.quote: DNS traffic steering selects destinations returned in answers. Failover changes the selected destination after failure.
For east and west endpoints, a separate health check and policy, or an operator, must detect east's failure and change answers. Ordinary DNS records do not detect application health themselves.
A shared recursive resolver can reuse one answer for many clients, and each client may send many requests using that address or connection.
After east is removed from new answers, cached clients can still try it. Existing connections do not migrate to west just because DNS changed.
West must be reachable, healthy and have enough spare capacity for redirected work.

answers.answer: An open connection can keep working without another lookup; a usable cached address can also permit a new connection during a DNS outage. New users without such reuse need a reachable recursive resolver, working delegation and authoritative servers that answer, so they can fail while existing users continue. Start with the client's recursive resolver: inspect the actual queried name and type, answer or error, and remaining TTL. Compare authoritative data and parent delegation when results are wrong or failing. An authority's new address alongside a cached old one suggests cache age rather than an automatic record edit. Once the expected address is obtained, inspect connection, HTTPS and application results separately. HTTP 500 means an HTTP service responded with an error; that alone is not a DNS lookup failure, and successful DNS does not prove Notes works. Reachable alternate resolvers and authoritative servers reduce individual server failures but cannot fix shared bad records, broken delegation or a failed application. The scenario does not identify the exact DNS failure or the cause of the HTTP 500; those conclusions require the checks above.

evidence.quote: During a DNS outage, a client with a usable cached address may still connect, and an open connection may keep working without a lookup. Fresh uncached lookups need a reachable recursive resolver, working delegation and authoritative servers that can answer.

Start with the client's recursive resolver: inspect the queried name and type, its answer or error, and remaining TTL. Compare authoritative data and parent delegation when results are wrong or failing.
HTTP 500 means an HTTP service responded with an error; it is not by itself a DNS lookup failure.
Reachable alternate resolvers and authoritative servers reduce individual server failures. They cannot fix a shared wrong record, broken delegation or a failed application.

answers.answer: DNSSEC adds signatures to DNS data. A validating resolver checks them along a chain of trust beginning with a configured trusted key, with each trusted signing key vouching for the next link. Successful validation establishes the signed data's origin and integrity: alteration cannot go undetected. It does not encrypt or hide the query, certify Notes health, guarantee availability, or eliminate HTTPS certificate checks. HTTPS separately authenticates the endpoint through certificate validation and encrypts the HTTP exchange. The client must verify the requested hostname api.notes.example, even if DNS follows an alias to another name. Validation also does not grant application access permissions. No unsupported step is needed for these conclusions.

evidence.quote: DNSSEC adds signatures to DNS data. A validating resolver checks those signatures through a chain of trust: each trusted signing key vouches for the next link, starting at a configured trusted key. Successful validation establishes the signed data's origin and integrity, meaning it has not been altered without detection.
DNSSEC does not encrypt the query, certify service health or guarantee availability.

HTTPS separately authenticates the endpoint through certificate validation and encrypts the HTTP exchange. The client must still verify the certificate for the hostname it requested, api.example.test, even if DNS followed an alias to edge.example.test.
A valid DNSSEC answer does not remove HTTPS certificate checks.
